title: The Witness of God: Scripture's Self-Attestation
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Ground of Biblical Authority
subpoints: Authority depends wholly on God, not human or church testimony
Confirming evidences (history, prophecy) are secondary to divine origin
The Holy Spirit provides the inward assurance of Scripture's truth

outline.title: The Logic of Self-Attestation
subpoints: No higher authority exists to verify the Bible if it is God's Word
Circular reasoning is a logical necessity when the source is the ultimate truth
Calvin’s analogy: Light cannot be verified by darkness

outline.title: Scripture’s Self-Description
subpoints: Prophetic formula: 'Thus says the Lord' indicates relayed speech, not human insight
The Bible is not human words endorsed by God, but God’s words spoken through humans

outline.title: The Mechanism of Inspiration
subpoints: Prophecy is not of private interpretation
Human authors were moved by the Holy Spirit like a sailboat by the wind
The New Testament recognized itself as Scripture within the first century

summary:
This sermon introduces a five-part series on the reliability of Scripture, beginning with the foundational argument that the Bible is reliable primarily because God is its author. Pastor Lyro argues that while historical evidence, fulfilled prophecy, and internal consistency serve as confirming proofs, they are not the ultimate ground of faith. Instead, the authority of Scripture rests wholly on God, who is truth itself, and the inward witness of the Holy Spirit in the believer’s heart. This perspective aligns with the Westminster Confession of Faith and the theology of John Calvin, who emphasized that Scripture is self-authenticating.

The session addresses the logical challenge of circular reasoning by asserting that if the Bible is the highest source of truth, it must be the standard by which its own truth is verified, as no higher authority exists. Using Calvin’s analogy, the pastor explains that asking for external verification of Scripture is like asking darkness to define light; light is self-evident. The sermon emphasizes that the Bible’s claim to be God’s word is not a human invention but a divine declaration.

Finally, the sermon examines how Scripture describes itself. It highlights the prophetic formula 'Thus says the Lord,' indicating that the prophets were relaying divine speech rather than offering personal insight. Citing 2 Timothy 3:16, the pastor explains the Greek term 'Theopneustos' (God-breathed) to illustrate that the Bible is the product of God’s breath, not human words later endorsed by God. The discussion concludes with 2 Peter, noting that the New Testament authors recognized their writings as Scripture, affirming the divine origin and authority of the entire canon.
